title: Redwood POC Weekly Sync - Benchmark Review vs Baseline Provider
next_steps: Redwood to share updated benchmark spreadsheet with per-model latency/throughput across payload sizes
Sentinel to run 1-off baseline test on their staging infra and share logs
Schedule canary deployment discussion next Tues 2025-07-01
action_items: Maya Chen: Share annotated benchmark CSV and config used (batch sizes, quantization) - due 2025-06-27
Liam O'Neill: Produce recommended Redwood Dedicated config (GPU type, batch config, autoscale policy) - due 2025-06-30
Priya Nair: Provide sample production prompt set + 1000 sample requests for latency reproducibility - due 2025-06-28
Carlos Vega: Export staging network egress metrics and baseline provider logs - due 2025-06-29
summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark results vs the customer's current baseline provider. Redwood presented latency/throughput numbers across 3 model variants and payload sizes; discussion covered differences in batching, KV cache behavior, and network variability. Customer raised concerns around tail latency, VPC egress, and encryption keys. Agreed next steps to share annotated benchmark sheet, run a staging baseline test, and plan canary deployment details.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, Liam is with me on the SE side. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Aisha Rahman: Aisha here. Carlos and Priya on from Sentinel.
[00:12] Carlos Vega: Yup hi, Carlos.
[00:14] Priya Nair: Priya here.
[00:16] Maya Chen: Great. We'll go through the benchmark deck then walk through differences vs your baseline provider. Aim to keep it to about 30 minutes and leave time for q's.
[00:27] Liam O'Neill: Quick note, some of the numbers we sent are for single-node Redwood Dedicated configs and others are hosted, so I'll call out which is which as we go.
[00:36] Aisha Rahman: Sounds good. We're mostly interested in p95 and p99 since our SLA is user-facing — want to avoid bad tail latency.
[00:44] Maya Chen: Totally. OK slide 1, high level summary: across the standard 8k-token Llama-variant tests we saw median (p50) token latency about 12 ms on Redwood Dedicated (A100x) vs 18 ms on baseline provider; p95 38 ms vs 65 ms; p99 120 ms vs 210 ms. These are with continuous KV caching enabled and batch size tuned to 8 for the workload.
[01:10] Priya Nair: Wait those p99 numbers look much better — what exactly did you configure for the baseline? The baseline numbers we have seem different.
[01:18] Liam O'Neill: Good question. For baseline we used the numbers you provided from last week — note that provider reported numbers were on a multi-tenant pool with dynamic CPU/GPU sharing. Also baseline ran without prefix cache for the chat-like prompt sets; that impacts tail heavily on repeated contexts.
[01:33] Priya Nair: Hmm we didn't realize the cache difference. Our baseline tests were more focused on raw single-request latency.
[01:39] Maya Chen: Right, so two confounding factors: caching and batching. In our experiments we kept a KV cache warm with the typical conversation prefixes you gave and used Redwood's continuous batching window tuned to 30 ms. That reduces p99 significantly for conversational workloads.
[01:54] Carlos Vega: Can you explain continuous batching? In our staging env we saw large variance when traffic bursts came in.
[02:00] Liam O'Neill: Sure — continuous batching holds requests for up to the batching window (30 ms here) to form larger batches. It trades a few ms of added queuing for much higher throughput and lower per-token cost. For bursty traffic we have autoscale policies to spin up more Dedicated workers to prevent long queues; we can show the policy we recommend.
[02:21] Aisha Rahman: What about tail events — say p99+ where network egress spikes — is that mostly infra or model?
[02:28] Maya Chen: Often a mix. We saw several tail events in your baseline logs that correlated with VPC egress throttling on the provider side and also with cold KV cache misses. When we isolate network variability in our controlled tests, Redwood Dedicated still holds lower p99 thanks to more consistent GPU assignment and KV cache locality.
[02:47] Priya Nair: You mentioned GPU types — were those A100s on Redwood and what about gridded instances?
[02:53] Liam O'Neill: For the Dedicated numbers in the spreadsheet we used A100 80GB for the larger model and T4s for smaller variants in a quantized path — we included both so you can compare. Quantization also reduced memory pressure and lowered latency in some cases, but accuracy tradeoffs were noted in the notes column.
[03:12] Carlos Vega: The spreadsheet had a few columns I didn't fully parse — could you walk through the column mapping?
[03:16] Maya Chen: Absolutely: columns are model_variant, payload_tokens, batch_size, kv_cache (on/off), quantization_profile, p50, p95, p99, throughput_rps, measured_cost_per_token. We'll attach an annotated version after the call.
[03:29] Aisha Rahman: On cost, how are you measuring measured_cost_per_token? Our finance team wants deterministic comparisons to baseline.
[03:36] Liam O'Neill: It's normalized cost based on GPU-hour rate plus amortized infra overhead — we included the raw GPU cost assumptions in the notes. For Dedicated we showed reserved capacity pricing which pushes down per-token costs vs on-demand. We'll include both on-demand and reserved columns.
[03:51] Priya Nair: Our baseline provider quoted us a reserved price too and their p95 was similar in some cases — where did we pull the biggest gap from?
[03:58] Maya Chen: Biggest gaps were on chatting conversational long-context workloads where KV caching and kernel selection really matter. For single-shot classification the gap narrows. Also network topology: when the baseline was sending requests across regions we saw added latency.
[04:13] Carlos Vega: Did you run any tests that replicate our staging network conditions specifically (NAT, VPC subnet, egress through gateway)?
[04:20] Liam O'Neill: We ran a subset of tests from an environment that mimics your staging NAT and egress; results are in sheet tab "staging-sim". There are still differences because we couldn't run inside your actual VPC. That's why we asked you to run the 1-off baseline staging test and share logs.
[04:36] Priya Nair: Ok makes sense. For the p99 gaps can you show where KV misses happened in the trace?
[04:41] Liam O'Neill: Yes we have sample traces attached. You'll see KV miss events aligned with larger decode times. When cache is cold the first few requests in a conversation pay the cost.
[04:51] Aisha Rahman: Encryption/KMS — our security team wants to ensure keys never leave our control. How would Redwood handle that in Dedicated or Private?
[04:58] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS integration and HSM attachments for Private. We can share the SOC2 + KMS integration docs. Key material never leaves the HSM boundary in the Private offering; Dedicated can be configured to use your KMS over a VPC endpoint.
[05:13] Carlos Vega: Any notes on logging and audit trails? We need request-level traceability for HIPAA audits.
[05:19] Liam O'Neill: We have per-request tracing and request IDs surfaced in the Console. For Private deployments those logs can be stored in your S3/bucket with retention policy you control. We'll share the audit logging playbook.
[05:31] Maya Chen: Quick poll \u0011 does Sentinel want Redwood to prioritize lower p99 (tuning cache/batch) or minimize cost further?
[05:38] Aisha Rahman: Priority is p99 for now, we'll optimize cost after SLA is satisfied.
[05:42] Priya Nair: Agreed. Also we want to run a small canary in staging to validate actual tail behavior.
[05:47] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Proposed canary: 5% traffic, dedicated workers w/ KV cache warmers, run for 48 hours and collect p50/p95/p99 and trace logs. We'll draft the canary plan.
[05:58] Carlos Vega: About warmers \u0011 how invasive are they? We don't want synthetic traffic mixing with real user telemetry.
[06:04] Liam O'Neill: Warmers can be run from a separate namespace; they drop into the same cache population without touching production logs. Configurable frequency and scope. We'll provide a non-intrusive recipe.
[06:16] Aisha Rahman: OK let's recap next steps.
[06:19] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to share annotated benchmarks + raw config, Sentinal to run 1-off baseline staging test and share logs, Redwood to craft canary plan and Dedicated config recommendation, schedule canary planning call for 2025-07-01.
[06:36] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone.
[06:38] Carlos Vega: Thanks.
[06:39] Aisha Rahman: Bye.
[06:40] Maya Chen: Thanks all, bye.
